hero.title: Rainwater butt and tank
hero.subtitle: Free rainwater harvesting calculator from your roof and local rainfall, in France, Switzerland and Luxembourg.

intro.title: Rainwater harvesting: from a water butt to a tank
intro.body: WaterPulse estimates how much water a roof can collect and which rainwater tank fits. A water butt is that collection path — downpipe, filter, storage — whether it feeds a small garden barrel or a tank of several thousand litres. Enter a place in France, Switzerland, Luxembourg or elsewhere, the roof area, the household size and the uses (garden, toilet, laundry). The calculation uses Open-Meteo rainfall and suggests a volume close to a 21-day reserve. The same form covers the whole range.

how.title: How do you size a rainwater butt or tank?
how.lead: The calculation needs three inputs: the roof, local rainfall, and the uses rainwater can actually cover. The volume is then compared with common sizes, from 300 L to 10,000 L.

steps.title: 1. Locate your roof
steps.body: Pick a country and a city, or drop a point on the map. WaterPulse loads average rainfall (mm/year) from Open-Meteo for that exact place, not a national average.

steps.title: 2. Describe the roof, household and uses
steps.body: Enter the area in m², the roof type (tiles, flat, metal) and how many people live there. Tick garden, toilets and laundry: only those uses count as demand, and they are not all allowed in the same way.

steps.title: 3. Read the tank volume
steps.body: The calculator shows collectable water, demand and a tank rounded to a common size, with a rough autonomy figure. How to choose between a water butt and a cistern is just below.

sizing.title: What size rainwater butt or tank should you choose?
sizing.lead: There is no standard tank. The right volume is one the roof can fill and that you use before the next real spell of rain. A water butt of a few hundred litres waters a garden. A tank of several thousand litres starts to cover toilets.
sizing.compare: A rainwater butt is most often an above-ground tank under a downpipe. Service Public also describes a buried tank, usually with more capacity, whether or not it is connected inside the house. These ranges help you read the result. They are not a price: cost depends on the model, the installation and the municipality, and WaterPulse does not estimate it.

factors.title: Roof area
factors.body: Use the roof footprint in m². One millimetre of rain on 1 m² is 1 litre, but not all of it reaches the tank: tiles, a flat roof and metal do not run off the same way, and the calculation keeps about 10% back for filtration.

factors.title: Local rainfall
factors.body: The same roof in Brest and in Sion will not fill the same tank. Across France, Switzerland and Luxembourg, totals also change a lot from one town to the next. The calculator uses the Open-Meteo series for the point you pick.

factors.title: How you use the water
factors.body: The suggested volume covers about 21 days, based on whichever is smaller: water the roof can collect over the year, or your demand. There is no point storing more than the roof supplies, or much more than you use between wet periods.

sizes.body: Above-ground water butt for a shed or a small terrace. Enough for occasional watering, too small for toilets all year.
A house with a garden, or toilets only. Often the first step beyond a butt on a downpipe.
A household combining toilets and watering, sometimes laundry, with a roof of about 50 to 100 m² in a moderately wet area.
A large roof, or a wish to last longer without rain. At this size people usually move to a cistern, sometimes buried.

sizing.note: Two 80 m² roofs do not need the same tank if one is in Luxembourg and the other in Valais. These ranges place the result; they do not replace it.

usage.title: Water use per person and tank size
usage.lead: Water use per person only matters here for the uses rainwater can cover. It does not tell you which tank to buy.

points.title: Tap water, in France
points.body: In 2022, average domestic drinking-water use in France was about 150 litres per person per day, or 54.6 m³ a year (SISPEA, summarised on notre-environnement.gouv.fr). That is potable water. The average hides large gaps between departments, and some of the volume labelled domestic can come from small non-household activities.

points.title: What a tank does not replace
points.body: Drinking, cooking, dishwashing and washing yourself stay on the drinking-water supply. Sizing a rainwater butt as if it had to provide those 150 litres per person makes the tank larger than the roof can fill, and larger than the rules allow.

points.title: What the calculator counts
points.body: The household-size field only multiplies the uses you tick: 25 litres per person per day for toilets, 15 litres for laundry. The garden is a flat 60 litres per day for the household, not per person. The suggested tank is then about 21 days of reserve, capped by the water the roof actually collects.

usage.assumptions: The 25 L, 15 L and 60 L figures are WaterPulse assumptions for estimating demand, not a national statistic.

sources.label: Notre-environnement (French environment ministry), household drinking-water use

faq.title: Questions about the water butt and the tank
faq.lead: Rainwater harvesting, tank volume and rules of use in France, Switzerland and Luxembourg.

items.question: What is a rainwater butt?
items.answer: It is the equipment that collects water from a roof people cannot walk on, usually through the downpipes, and stores it in a tank. Service Public distinguishes a butt with no indoor connection, limited to outdoor uses, from one connected to the house for toilets, floor washing and laundry. The tank can sit above ground or be buried; a buried tank usually holds more. Some municipalities require a lid and mosquito protection. WaterPulse does not sell a model: it estimates the volume from your roof.

items.question: How does rainwater harvesting work?
items.answer: Water running off the roof is coarsely filtered, then stored in the tank. Over a year, collectable water equals area (m²) × local rainfall (mm) × a roof coefficient × 0.9. One millimetre on 1 m² is 1 litre. The calculator applies that formula to the point you place on the map, then suggests a reserve close to 21 days of use.

items.question: Does water use per person set the tank size?
items.answer: Only for the uses rainwater can cover. In France, domestic drinking-water use was about 150 litres per person per day in 2022, or 54.6 m³ a year (SISPEA). Drinking, cooking, dishes and personal washing do not go through the tank. The calculator uses 25 litres per person per day for toilets and 15 litres for laundry, plus 60 litres per day for the household garden. The roof then caps that demand.

items.question: How is collectable water calculated?
items.answer: Collectable water (L/year) = roof area (m²) × rainfall (mm) × roof coefficient × 0.9 (filtration). One millimetre on 1 m² equals 1 litre.

items.question: How is tank volume chosen?
items.answer: The recommended volume is about 21 days of reserve, based on the minimum of collectable water and yearly demand, then rounded to a common size between 300 L and 10,000 L.

items.question: How much rain falls in France, Switzerland and Luxembourg?
items.answer: The gap is often wider inside one country than between these three. In France, the Paris basin is often around 600 to 700 mm a year, the Atlantic coast and the mountains are wetter, and the Mediterranean rim is drier. In Switzerland, the Plateau is often near 1,000 mm, the Alps wetter, and some valleys such as parts of Valais much drier. Luxembourg is more like 800 to 1,000 mm, a little higher in the Oesling than in the Gutland. These are orders of magnitude: for a tank, rainfall at the exact point matters more than the country average. The calculator asks Open-Meteo for the place you choose.

items.question: What can rainwater be used for, and which rules apply?
items.answer: Rainwater collected from a roof is not drinking water. In France, Service Public (page “Récupération de l'eau de pluie”, checked on 12 December 2025) distinguishes two cases. With no indoor connection: watering, outdoor cleaning, washing a vehicle at home, and a decorative fountain not meant for drinking. With a connection: toilets, floor washing and laundry. It is still forbidden to drink it, cook with it, wash dishes or wash yourself. The pipes must stay separate from drinking water, labelled “non-potable water”, and a connected system is declared at the town hall. That framework comes from decree no. 2024-796 and the order of 12 July 2024, which replaced the order of 21 August 2008. In Switzerland, watering and often toilets are accepted, but building rules depend on the canton and the municipality. In Luxembourg, garden use is common; use inside the house must stay separate from drinking water and follow municipal rules. The local water service is the reference. WaterPulse estimates a volume; it does not approve an installation.

items.question: Water butt, tank or cistern: which one?
items.answer: A water butt is usually an above-ground tank, from a few hundred litres to about 1,000 L, fed by a downpipe and meant mainly for the garden. A cistern is several thousand litres, often up to 10,000 L, sometimes buried, when toilets or a longer reserve come into play. The right choice is the volume the roof can fill and that you use before the water sits for too long.

items.question: Is the calculation the same in France, Switzerland and Luxembourg?
items.answer: Yes for the formula: roof area, local rainfall, roof type and uses. What changes is the rainfall total at that place and the rules of use, not a constant per country. A roof in Lille, Geneva or Luxembourg City is calculated the same way once the point is on the map.

items.question: Is rainwater safe to drink?
items.answer: Not as collected. Without treatment designed for drinking water, it stays non-potable. WaterPulse sizes uses such as the garden or toilets. A drinking-water project has to be checked by a professional and against local rules.

items.question: Where does the rainfall data come from?
items.answer: Averages come from the Open-Meteo Archive API (several years of history) for the latitude and longitude you choose.

items.question: Do the results replace a professional study?
items.answer: No. This is an estimate to prepare a water butt or a cistern. A site survey is still needed for a final design, especially if the tank is buried or connected to the house.

sections.heading: 1. Who we are
paragraphs: WaterPulse (https://waterpulse.maketru.com) is a free online rainwater harvesting and tank sizing calculator.

sections.heading: 2. Data collected
paragraphs: When you use the calculator, technical parameters (latitude, longitude, area, uses) are sent to our server and Open-Meteo to fetch rainfall. This data is not used to identify you personally.
